items.readable_text:
Content:
A combination is a selection of objects in which order does not matter. Two selections of the same items are always counted as the same selections, even if the items are in a different order.

Content:
For example, suppose we have [MATH: 5] books but can only take [MATH: 3] of them on a trip. How many combinations are there? In other words, how many ways can we take [MATH: 3] of the books?

Content:
First, recall that the total number of ways of selecting [MATH: 3] books from [MATH: 5] (where order matters) is given by the permutation [MATH: {}_5P_3{:}]
[MATH: _{5}P_{3}|= (5!)/((5 − 3)!); = (5!)/(2!); = 60]
However, the permutation calculation [MATH: {}_5P_3] assumes that order of selection matters, but in our problem order is not important. Regardless of the order in which we choose the books, the chosen books are coming with us on the trip and the rest of the books will be left behind.

Content:
So, we must divide by the number of ways to order the [MATH: 3] books that we selected, which is [MATH: 3!.] Doing this, we get

Content:
[MATH: (_{5}P_{3})/(3!)|= (60)/(3!); = (60)/(6); = 10.]

Content:
Therefore, there are [MATH: 10] ways that we can take [MATH: 3] of the books with us.

The number of combinations of [MATH: n] objects taken [MATH: r] at a time is given by the formula [MATH: {}_nC_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!r!}.]

[MATH: \require{cancel} \eqalign{ {}_{7}C_5 &= \dfrac {7!} {(7 - 5)!5!} \[5pt] &= \dfrac {7!} {2!5!} \[5pt] &= \dfrac {7 \cdot 6 \cdot \cancel{5!}} {2!\cancel{5!}} \[5pt] &= \dfrac {7 \cdot 6 } {2 \cdot 1 } \[5pt] & = \dfrac {42}{2} \[5pt] &= 21. }]
